extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal practitioners, and scholars of English common law
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of English common-law principles governing parental duties and powers, legitimacy and bastardy, guardianship and infancy, and the basic nature and purpose of corporations. Useful as a reference for interpreting status, capacity, and fiduciary duties under historic/common-law rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental duty to provide suitable education
rubrics_metrics.description: The last duty of parents to their children is that of giving them an education suitable to their station in life: a duty pointed out by reason, and of far the greatest importance of any.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to educate a child renders the benefit of being brought into the world questionable. Municipal laws often fail to compel education; statutes for apprenticing poor children provide public means to ensure training. The rich are largely left to their own option except in matters of religion (see statutory restrictions on sending children abroad for popish instruction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory penalties for sending children abroad for popish instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: If any person sends any child under his government beyond the seas to be instructed, persuaded, or strengthened in the popish religion, the parent or person sending shall forfeit £100 (statutory penalty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional disabilities attach: the person sending or sent may be disabled to sue or hold office, enjoy legacies, or be executor/administrator; may forfeit goods and real estate for life. Penalties specified by Stat. 11 & 12 W. III. c. 4 and Stat. 3 Car. I. c. 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source and scope of parental power
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of parents over their children is derived from their duty to the child; authority is given partly to enable performance of duty and partly as recompense for care and trouble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different systems allocate different extents of authority (e.g., Roman patria potestas extreme; English law more moderate). Parental power includes rights necessary to secure education and protection; subject to legal limits and fiduciary duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental right to correct children reasonably
rubrics_metrics.description: A parent may lawfully correct his child, being under age, in a reasonable manner; for this is for the benefit of his education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonableness is the limiting standard; historical examples show indulgence toward parental affections but not unlimited violence (see cases distinguishing manslaughter from murder in parental reprisals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental consent required for minor's marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: The consent or concurrence of the parent to the marriage of his child under age was directed by ancient law to be obtained; now it is absolutely necessary; for without it the contract is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule protects minors from early/precipitate marriages and from artful persons seeking to exploit them; statutory citation: Stat. 26 Geo. II. c. 33.

rubrics_metrics.name: Father's fiduciary role over a minor's estate
rubrics_metrics.description: A father has no other power over his son's estate than as his trustee or guardian; though he may receive the profits during the child's minority, yet he must account for them when he comes of age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The father's benefit of a child's labour while maintained is likened to rights of masters over apprentices/servants; accountability on reaching majority is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termination and delegation of parental power
rubrics_metrics.description: Parental power over the person ceases at twenty one; parents may appoint guardians by will; they may delegate part of their authority during life to tutors or schoolmasters who act in loco parentis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parental empire continues after death via testamentary guardians. Delegates (tutors/schoolmasters) have authority of restraint and correction necessary for their roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children's duties to parents (obedience and maintenance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Children owe subjection and obedience during their minority, and honour and reverence ever after; those who gave us existence are entitled to protection in their infirmity and to maintenance if in need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These duties proceed from natural justice and retribution; English law enforces them (e.g., Stat. 43 Eliz. c. 2) and, except for spurious children, does not dissolve filial obligation due to parental misbehaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a bastard under English law
rubrics_metrics.description: A bastard, by our English laws, is one that is not only begotten, but born, out of lawful matrimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike civil/canon law, English law requires birth after lawful wedlock (not merely legitimation by subsequent marriage). Reasons include certainty of parentage and prevention of frauds; historical parliamentary practice (Parliament of Merton) rejected legitimation by subsequent marriage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumptions and rules affecting legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: During coverture access of the husband shall be presumed (praesumitur pro legitimatione), unless the contrary can be shown; but where the husband has been absent extra quatuor maria for above nine months, issue shall be bastard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions include uncertainty of gestation after husband's death (few days allowed); writ de ventre inspiciendo to examine widow suspected of feigning pregnancy; divorce a mensa et thoro produces bastardy for children born during separation; divorce a vinculo matrimonii renders issue born during coverture bastards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and procedural maintenance for bastards
rubrics_metrics.description: English law provides maintenance for bastards: when a woman declares herself with child and charges a person by oath before a justice of the peace, the justice may apprehend that person until he gives security to maintain the child or appear at quarter sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the woman dies/marries before delivery or proves not pregnant, the accused is discharged. Sessions or two justices can order payment; overseers may seize rents/goods if putative father or mother absconds. A woman cannot be compelled to name the father until one month after delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights and incapacities of a bastard (inheritance and settlement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bastard can acquire rights but cannot inherit; being filius nullius he is of kin to nobody. He may gain a surname by reputation; his settlement is in the parish where born, for he hath no father.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In fraud cases settlement rules vary (e.g., illegally removed women). Historically bastards were barred from certain ecclesiastical dignities, though that doctrine is now largely obsolete. Legitimization and capacity to inherit require an act of parliament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardianship: species and appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: Several species of guardians exist: guardians by nature (father and sometimes mother), guardians for nurture (father/mother until 14), guardians in socage (common-law guardians from next of kin), guardians by statute or testament (appointed by deed or will), and special guardians by custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guardians in socage take place when the minor is entitled to estate in lands and are selected to avoid conflict of interest with heirs. Statutory guardianship (e.g., statute 12 Car. II. c. 24) allows a father to appoint custody by deed or will to any person except a popish recusant until the child attains 21.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardian's powers, duties and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The power and reciprocal duty of a guardian and ward are the same, pro tempore, as that of a father and child; the guardian when the ward comes of age is bound to give an account and must answer for losses by wilful default or negligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid disputes, guardians of large estates often apply to the court of chancery for direction and account annually. The lord chancellor is the general and supreme guardian of infants, idiots, and lunatics; Chancery may remove abusive guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ages for legal capacities (male and female)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific ages define capacities: male—12 may take the oath of allegiance; 14 years of discretion (consent to marriage, choose guardian, testament if proved); 17 may be an executor; 21 full age. Female—7 betrothed; 9 entitled to dower; 12 years maturity (consent to marriage, testament if proved); 14 legal discretion (choose guardian); 17 executrix; 21 dispose of self and lands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full age is 21 completed on the day preceding the anniversary of birth. Ages vary by jurisdiction (e.g., Scotland agrees with England; Naples 18; France marriage capacity at 30; Holland 25).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infants' civil and criminal disabilities and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Infants have privileges and disabilities: generally cannot be sued except with guardian; may sue by guardian or prochein amy; under seven cannot be capitally punished; between seven and fourteen may be doli capax if they can discern right and wrong; generally cannot alien or make binding deeds, but with many exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions include: infant trustees or mortgagees may convey under chancery/exchequer direction; an infant with an advowson may present to a benefice; an infant may purchase land and later confirm or disavow on majority; an infant may bind himself apprentice by indenture; may by deed or will appoint a guardian to his children; may be bound for necessaries and for good teaching and instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and legal characteristics of corporations
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial persons (bodies politic or corporate) are constituted to maintain perpetual succession and legal immortality so that particular rights and immunities can be preserved for public advantage (e.g., colleges for religion and learning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporations act as one person in law with one will determined by majority; they can establish rules and statutes, retain privileges and property in perpetuity without endless conveyances, and defend their privileges collectively. Origin traced to Roman and canon law; corporations solve the practical problems of continuity and governance for collective purposes.
